3.7 Higher Plant Cells versus Animal Cells

Learning Outcome

  1. List three features of cell structure that make plant cells different from animal cells.
  2. Explain how differences in plant and animal cells cause them to communicate differently.

All animals have either internal or external skeletons or skeletonlike systems to support their tissues. Animal cells do not have cell walls; instead, the plasma membrane, called the cell membrane by most zoologists (animal scientists), forms the outer boundary of animal cells. Higher plant cells have walls that are thickened and rigid to varying degrees, with a framework of cellulose fibrils. Higher plant cells also have plasmodesmata connecting the protoplasts with each other through microscopic holes in the walls. Animal cells lack plasmodesmata, because they have no walls. When higher plant cells divide, a cell plate is formed during the telophase of mitosis, but cell plates do not form in animal cells, which divide by pinching in two.

Other differences are due to the presence or absence of certain organelles. Centrioles, for example, the tiny, paired, keg-shaped structures found just outside the nucleus, occur in all animal cells but are generally absent from higher plant cells. Plastids, common in plant cells, are not found in animal cells. Vacuoles, which are often large in plant cells, are either small or absent in animal cells.
